strengths: Clear identification of a genuine research gap: the paper convincingly argues (Table 1, related work) that existing methods either estimate CATE magnitudes or use non-orthogonal ranking objectives, and positions Rank-Learner as the first model-agnostic two-stage learner that is both direct (ranking) and Neyman-orthogonal.

Careful and complete theory: the efficient influence function of the pairwise loss is derived from first principles (Appendix C), Neyman-orthogonality is proven rigorously for all three nuisance components, and the population optima of all four objectives are characterized (Theorem 5.2, Appendix D), including a thoughtful analysis of the smoothing parameter kappa and its bias-variance trade-off.

Extensive and well-designed experiments: fully synthetic benchmark with varying n and overlap, three semi-synthetic benchmarks with realistic covariates, the real-world CRITEO uplift benchmark, plus additional ACIC/IHDP evaluations, sensitivity analyses (kappa, nuisance misspecification, pseudo-label clipping, pair subsampling), and additional strong baselines (FlexTENet, PairNet, tree ranker) in the appendix.

Fair comparison methodology: identical architectures and training budgets across methods, with ablations that cleanly disentangle the effect of (i) direct ranking vs. CATE estimation and (ii) orthogonal vs. plug-in objectives; the plug-in ranker is a well-chosen ablation baseline.
Good presentation quality, honest discussion of practical issues (pseudo-label clipping, computational cost of pairwise training, role of kappa), and available code.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is fairly incremental: it applies the standard one-step/influence-function orthogonalization recipe (Kennedy 2024; Foster & Syrkanis 2023) to a pairwise soft ranking loss. The novelty lies in the combination and the derivation, not in a new learning principle.

There is a conceptual tension between the motivation and the theory: the paper motivates ranking as an 'easier' problem that avoids recovering CATE magnitudes, yet the population minimizer of the orthogonal loss is g = tau/kappa + c (Theorem 5.2), i.e., a scaled CATE. The orthogonality is achieved precisely because the smooth surrogate reintroduces dependence on effect magnitudes, so the practical benefit of 'not solving the harder problem' is weaker than claimed. The kappa analysis acknowledges this, but the framing in the abstract/introduction oversells it.

Empirical gains are modest and often within one standard deviation: e.g., on semi-synthetic benchmarks Rank-Learner's improvements over DR-learner and plug-in ranker are small (1.35 vs 1.34 on MovieLens; 1.18 vs 1.17 on MIMIC-III), and on the synthetic benchmark at n=2000 methods converge. No statistical significance tests are reported for the main comparisons; only 5 seeds are used.

The binary ranking loss L_bin (the most direct formalization of 'pure ranking') is not orthogonal, and the paper does not fully resolve why orthogonalizing the softer surrogate is the right design rather than, e.g., an orthogonal version based on a different ranking objective; the choice is justified post hoc via the influence function derivability.

Evaluation of AUTOC relies on an approximation of Chernozhukov et al. (2025) for unobserved treatment effects in semi-synthetic settings, and the real-world CRITEO experiment induces confounding synthetically, so the strongest claims about observational settings rest partly on simulated confounding.
Some references are unusual (e.g., ICML 2026 and 2026 journal citations), and the paper lacks a dedicated limitations section beyond the impact statement.
